item.description: + a retrospective, not in that order
item.content:encoded:
Are you interested in helping more people transition into AI safety? 💖

Well, you’re in luck! In this issue:

  • A Retrospective: some reflections on the week

  • Context Week Connections: the bios of 10 people from Context Week who are transitioning into AI safety, how you can help them, and their contact information

A Brief Retrospective

  • Context Week ended up being much more successful than I anticipated, but not necessarily for reasons of “giving people context.” Instead, I think the greatest value of Context Week came in the 1-on-1 career guidance we gave participants, and the immersive community experience.

    • We had participants ranging from 15 to 800 hours of exposure to / involvement in AI safety; for those on the latter end of the spectrum, I was worried they wouldn’t find much value in e.g. reading AI 2040.

    • However, those folks often came into Context Week with some specific uncertainties they wanted to chat through, e.g. what org would be the best fit for me? Would it be more valuable to work at CAISI or METR? How do I go from “I lurk on LessWrong and read a bunch of AI safety stuff” to “I seriously want to work in the space full time”?

    • For these kinds of folks in particular, having 1-on-1 chats with facilitators was a huge value add: we talked through specific cruxes and connected them with relevant people.

  • With that said, given how much value there was in 1-on-1 advising, I’m sad to see that BlueDot no longer does 1-on-1 calls with people! Their advising page is now solely dedicated to Career Transition Grants. However, there are still orgs that offer this service; I’ll list a few below in case useful:

    • 80,000 Hours — “free, personalised advice on your highest-impact career”

    • Successif — mid-career and senior professionals, with a particular focus on AI safety

    • Probably Good — for all experience levels

    • Impact First — UK, students

  • I’m really excited by the number of people who, post-Context Week, took concrete steps in the direction of full-time AIS roles! I’ve been having follow-up calls with some of the participants, and it’s been lovely to see.

  • For some reason, we had a bunch of speakers flake at the last minute, rip. I don’t really know why this is, but found it disappointing!

  • I think the event could have gone better with slightly more prep (my understanding is that this was organized in the span of a couple of weeks, or less?) because there were some points at which the draft syllabus didn’t seem super valuable to me. That said, I’m grateful that Harry gave me executive control over how to steer my group (so I ended up just doing my own thing at some points, which went well I think lol).

  • A suggestion for next time: Make a site like Praxis and give attendees + speakers access to bios beforehand (maybe also use an AI tool to pair up people who would benefit most from speaking to each other).

  • Another suggestion: “Context Week” as a name is fine, but perhaps something like “Transition Week” would be more accurate? (Def continue workshopping that haha)

another way to get context :)

Context Week Connections 🌷

Some lovely people from BlueDot’s context week are looking to meet others in AI safety – for advice, collaborations, roles, etc. If you work at one of the orgs they mention, or know someone who does, it would be really lovely if you’d reach out and help guide them as they navigate the field!

Christine Corry

Bio: Christine just graduated from UC Berkeley with degrees in Computer Science and Astrophysics. She is currently a Second Look Research Fellow at UChicago’s XLab, replicating empirical AI safety research (no-CoT evals and emergent misalignment work). She’s built internal LLM-based tooling for Apple, trained DNA prediction LLMs at the Innovative Genomics Institute, and spent three years studying pilot cognition at NASA. She’s increasingly convinced that frontier AI policy would be higher leverage and better suited to her skillset as a communicator energized by interpersonal work and focused on translating technical concepts for general audiences.

Looking to meet: Specific orgs: Encode AI, SAIP, CAISI, other think tanks, people actively working in politics, Horizon, GovAI, IAPS (just applied to their special projects role and very excited about my fit for that). Generally: macro-strategy and US-China people.

Roles of interest: Politics directly (think tank, congressional staff, advocacy), strengthening DC–Bay Area communications (special projects type role), general field building.

Contact: christinecorry1405@gmail.com

Ishaan Makkar

Bio: I studied physics at Imperial College London and co-founded Hexa, where I built and sold B2B AI products and helped scale the business to $16k MRR. I’m now exploring AI safety research, particularly RL environments for misalignment, evaluation and monitoring. I’d like to work with experienced researchers and find safety problems I could build a startup around.

Looking to meet: Researchers and engineers working on alignment, AI control, RL environments for misalignment, evaluations and monitoring. Nonprofits I’m interested in include Redwood Research, FAR.AI, METR, Alignment Research Center, the Center for AI Safety and Palisade Research. I’d also like to connect with MATS researchers and mentors, teams at Anthropic, OpenAI and Apollo Research, and RL-environment providers such as Surge AI or Scale AI.

I’d like to hear which problems these teams are struggling with and where I could contribute. I’d welcome research feedback or opportunities to collaborate, and conversations with founders working on AI safety.

Roles of interest: Research or engineering roles and collaborations in these areas, at either nonprofits or frontier labs. I’d like to work with people I can learn from and help build things that make AI systems safer. Longer term, I’m interested in building an AI-safety startup.

Contact: ishaan@hexaagents.com

Max Perin

Bio: I’m a recent grad (political science + philosophy at UCLA) who, until very recently, was committed to a very traditional prelaw track. I was heavily involved in competitive debate throughout high school and college, which led me to Praxis and then BlueDot’s context week, and I’ve been trying to pivot into AIS since.

Looking to meet: I’m most interested in policy research, think tank work, political advocacy, and potentially non-technical forecasting. Would love to chat further with folks from RAND and the AI Futures Project, and would be very interested in intros to people at AE Studio, FAI, and advocacy orgs that may not be on my radar.

Roles of interest: I have some background in nuclear policy/governance and have given a bit of thought to how that does/does not map onto potential governance regimes, but by and large I’m a generalist who’s probably best suited for roles that are highly analytical and where persuasive communication skills are a value add.

Contact: maxvperin12@gmail.com

Cat McGee

Bio: Software engineer focusing on cryptography (especially zero knowledge).

Looking to meet: People in the US or London (preferably London) working on or interested in verification of AI claims – software or hardware. Also interested in policy people who are trying to build towards Plan A.

Roles of interest: AI verification, but not sure of the specifics yet. “I might build something myself. I am currently interested in just expanding my network to learn and potentially partner with people in future; right now I will spend 6 months doing my own things (& maybe MATS).”

Contact: hello@mcgee.cat

Ray Che

Bio: I am a second-year CS PhD at UIUC working on AI and cybersecurity. I am interested in LLM security and adopting AI to secure systems. I received my BS and MS from Tsinghua University. My academic website is ray-che.com.

Looking to meet: Frontier AI security and control researchers and engineers at METR, Redwood, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Palo Alto.

Roles of interest: Security research scientists and engineers at frontier labs, Redwood/METR, and big techs.

Contact: xijiac2@illinois.edu

James Sykes

Bio: I’m a statistics PhD student at the University of Warwick working on cooperative AI with Dr Paolo Turrini and Prof Paul Jenkins. Currently, I’m doing a project on “Multi-Agent RL for Structured Population Dynamics”. After this, I’d like to work on personas and explore the use of methods from evolutionary biology to the selection and evaluation of LLMs. Outside of my PhD research, I’ve recently collaborated with UC Berkeley’s CLTC on cyber risk thresholds, as well as with SaferAI on risk modelling through SPAR.

Looking to meet:

  • People working on cooperative AI (including, but not restricted to, those associated with the Cooperative AI Foundation)

  • People at UK AISI working on multi-agent systems or risk modelling

  • People modelling loss-of-control dynamics using agent-based approaches

Roles of interest: An internship/fellowship in Spring/Summer 2027: MATS/ERA/Pivotal/similar, or directly at an org if I could find the right fit/funding.

Contact: jameslpsykes@gmail.com

Alex Chambers-Jones

Bio: I'm a British Physics undergraduate with a programming background and an interest in forecasting and strategy; I'd describe myself as a generalist. I previously researched AI translation, and I've spent the last year competing to build better AI forecasting systems; I'm in the top 5 in the Metaculus FutureEval tournament.

I've been following developments in AI safety since 2022, and since the Huggingface incident I've decided to transition as quickly as possible. I recently started a research project with James Sykes measuring safety-task sandbagging via activation steering.

Looking to meet:

  • Forecasting AI (e.g. Forethought, AI Futures Project)

  • Orgs working on alignment research, evaluations, etc. (e.g. Artificial Analysis) – I want to know where I can help given my previous experience (lots of work on LLMs, but no low-level technical ML/interpretability stuff)

Roles of interest:

  • Empirical safety research, particularly evaluations

  • Forecasting and strategy, particularly positive AI futures

Contact: alexcj2802@gmail.com

Jeremy Huff

Bio: I am an economics student with a public policy background who is interested in AI policy, regulation and governance. Would love to meet anyone who does more macro-level safety research and strategy.

Looking to meet: METR/Redwood/Encode, high-leverage AI safety organizations and policy.

Roles of interest: Interested in seeing orgs like METR grow into third-party auditors, and would love to apply policy/law lenses there.

Contact: jdhuff2048@gmail.com

Charlie Freiberg

Bio: Charlie Freiberg shapes the stories that make you known, understood, and chosen first. A narrative + communications strategist for founders and leaders, she translates innovations for the people who matter most, so you grow.

She is the cofounder of STUDY HALL, a creative building series where all disciplines play together with frontier partners (Plastic Labs, Collab Fund, Columbia University). She produces Story Is the Enzyme (raid, Edge Esmeralda), a talk series on how stories teach society to use tech responsibly – and Storyhack, a workshop for scaling your brand and business through self-discovery. She publishes xx, an advice column (💋) on finding what’s human while making the future.

Looking to meet: Comms leads from any and all orgs – even just for field building!

Roles of interest: Anthropic – unrivaled comms work at scale! Anyone across lab comms, and startups growing hard-to-explain things. Those running comms in safety (Seismic, METR, Apollo etc.). As a meta, anyone bringing the practice into the future with AI-native workflows.

Contact: charliejfreiberg@gmail.com

Daniel Hines

Bio: I’m a software engineer with a career in hard tech: counter-drone electronic warfare at Anduril, MRR spectroscopy at BrightSpec, blockchain protocol design at Marigold. I’m a full stack engineer (lowest-level firmware all the way to user-facing apps), and thrive in scrappy teams building something new. I use functional programming (Haskell, OCaml, Rust, Nix) and type theory for high-assurance software that can’t afford to fail.

I’m most excited about theoretical alignment research (agent foundations, deep learning theory, etc.), technical governance mechanisms for pause/pacing (e.g. verified inference) and LLM content detection.

Looking to meet: Orgs in theoretical alignment (met folks at Resolution and one guy at Iliad, but there’s probably more people/orgs I could meet). I’m also interested in formal methods for AI security. I think I could slot in as a generalist or research engineer into a lot of orgs.

Roles of interest: Any role at Resolution or Iliad (probably research engineering or generalist software engineering). I’m interested in meeting folks looking for technical cofounders.

Contact: d4hines@gmail.com

That’s everyone!

If someone above made you think “oh, they should talk to so-and-so” – it would be lovely if you’d send a quick email! It can be two lines.

And if you’re transitioning into AI safety and want to be featured in a future connections post, fill out this form! I might do this again, depending on how well things go.

Finally: thanks to Harry and Josh for a lovely time. You can read their write-up re: Context Week here.

item.title: AI safety needs a moonshot comms initiative
item.content:encoded:
Random life update: I have an X account now! My handle is @sophiekim_ai, until I find a better one (am open to suggestions!). Not sure how much I’ll end up using X, but you should follow me anyway <3

There are, broadly speaking, two ways to influence political change. You can either:

  1. Get people who are aligned with your views into positions of power (henceforth referred to as ‘placement’), or

  2. Attempt to influence those already in positions of power to be aligned (‘influence’). Concretely: in D.C., the former usually looks like running for office or being appointed to a position, while the latter is manifested in think tanks, nonprofits, and movements for social change.

The claims I’ll be making

  • The field of AI safety has mostly failed at placement,1 and hasn’t pursued influence aggressively enough.

    • I believe the field’s comparative advantage on ‘influence’ runs through voters, for reasons I’ll elaborate on in this post.

  • Industry2 has arguably succeeded quite a lot at placement (poster child: David Sacks), and their comparative advantage on ‘influence’ comes with lobbying (which is why they do so much of it).

  • Shockingly few people know the details of the Hugging Face attack outside AI safety circles.

    • As Ajeya Cotra says: “This might be the clearest warning shot we ever get.” We should make the most of it before it’s too late.

  • In addition to Hugging Face, there are currently a lot of concerns around AI that various different groups have, and I’m bullish on coalition-building.

    • I think a huge comms push could put a lot of unified momentum behind the favorable view of AI regulation that most Americans share – this is bipartisan!

  • On timing: The midterms are approaching, and I think now, post-Jacob Coxon,3 is a uniquely high-leverage time to do this kind of work.

  • The bottom line: We need a moonshot comms initiative ASAP.

The state of play

AI safety is a small field of various disparate organizations, up against huge corporations lobbying the White House with everything they’ve got. Jensen Huang, NVIDIA’s CEO, has been on the charm offensive for a long while; despite how hawkish Trump has historically been on China, it’s clearly been working.

Trump hates China! It’s basically his whole personality!! And yet, after Jensen paid for a $1-million-a-head dinner at Mar-a-Lago, what happened?

“[T]he White House reversed course on H20 chips, putting the plan for additional restrictions on hold… The planned American export controls on the H20 had been in the works for months, according to the two sources, and were ready to be implemented as soon as this week.”

—NPR

Earlier this year, Trump went a step further: he allowed H200s4 (different from H20s) to be sold to Chinese firms like Alibaba, Tencent, and Bytedance. The H200 is roughly six times as powerful as the H20, and it’s NVIDIA’s second most powerful chip.

The Trump administration talks constantly about “winning the AI race” against China; its former AI czar has cast safety advocates as the obstacle, accusing Anthropic of running a “sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering.” Trump himself even accuses folks in favor of pacing the frontier to be “playing right into the hands” of China.

But at the end of the day, who’s helping China speed up by letting them access the best American AI technology?

The irony is striking. Jensen warns that Western overregulation will make China win the AI race. And yet, NVIDIA’s actions under Jensen have probably helped speed up China far more than anything Dario Amodei (Anthropic’s CEO) – or anyone in favor of pacing the frontier, for that matter – has ever done.5

Trump says he’s beating China. On chips, he’s playing right into Jensen’s hands.

On comparative advantage

If you expect that the public will agree with you – if you’re “fighting the good fight,” so to speak – the thing you should probably do is to increase awareness of the issue you’re addressing so that people will be driven to actively prioritize supporting your cause. If you’re not acting in the interest of the American people, then you want to keep things as quiet as possible – or, when that fails, to change the subject.

Political scientists call the second mode “quiet politics”: organized interests tend to win on issues voters aren’t watching, and lose their grip once voters start paying attention.

Case studies

Perhaps the most obvious case study here is Big Oil. In 2009, at a time when climate legislation was ramping up, the American Petroleum Institute – rather than trying to convince voters about how great the oil industry is, actually – asked “oil companies to recruit employees, retirees and contractors to take part in rallies against climate change legislation.” Hello astroturfing!

More case studies, from the worlds of tobacco and broadband: In the 1990s, Philip Morris bankrolled a “National Smokers Alliance” covertly built by its PR firm. In 2017, the broadband industry paid for over 8.5 million fake comments urging the FCC to repeal net neutrality:

“The goal of the broadband industry campaign, according to internal documents the attorney general's office received, was to make it seem like there was "widespread grassroots support" for the repeal of net neutrality that could give the FCC chairman at the time, Ajit Pai, "volume and intellectual cover" for the repeal.”

Tobacco is an especially instructive (and hopefully inspirational!) case for AI safety, because the other side won. Anti-smoking advocates found they did best in local fights, where officials answered more directly to voters rather than tobacco money:

“There has been a striking increase in the adoption of local tobacco control ordinances during the past decade; by the end of 1995, approximately 1006 communities had enacted a local tobacco control ordinance. In response, the tobacco industry has advanced legislation in 29 states that preempts local authority to regulate tobacco.”

So, the tobacco industry’s response was to push state laws that stripped cities of the power to act at all. Woah! Sound familiar? Well, that might be because the tech industry is running the same play: preempt the states, where voters are closer to the fight.6

You can read more about how much the tech industry spends on lobbying here.

The public is on our side

In a June poll, 68% of respondents favored “a formal review process for the most advanced AI models before they can be widely released” – including most Republicans.

Indeed, polling from as early as January 2025 – conducted by the AI Policy Institute for Transformer – demonstrated widespread bipartisan support for government-mandated safety measures for AI companies:

And, as I wrote about in a previous post, there exists so much potential for aligning coalitions on this:

“You don’t need everyone to care about loss of control and superintelligence alignment. You need privacy advocates furious about AI-powered mass surveillance, environmentalists furious about illegal gas turbines poisoning children in Memphis, parents furious about chatbots encouraging their kids to kill themselves, women furious about Grok still making sexualized images of them, workers furious about displacement with no transition plan, national security people furious about chips being sold to adversaries, anti-war activists furious about Minab.”

68% of americans agree with this newsletter, most just don’t know it exists yet.

The time is now

(Well, actually, the time was ideally like 3 months ago, but anyway. You know what they say about planting trees!)

Things that are different now:

Jacob Coxon has triggered a preference cascade: he went viral on X, has been on virtually all the major media outlets: TIME, PBS, WSJ, Reuters, NBC, BBC, Fortune, The Guardian… the list goes on.

Also, now we have Hugging Face:

~1200 agents sent >70,000 messages and files on an unsanctioned message board, and ~700 attacked Hugging Face

Guys! 700 AI agents escaped their testing environment and coordinated to attack Hugging Face, and most of the world still doesn’t know! This is a bit crazy.7

We should fix that.

What might this look like?

Some very rough thoughts:

  • Hire some very competent political campaign managers, who are used to deploying hundreds of millions of dollars on advertisements and media.

    • Can we get David Plouffe or Jim Messina (Obama campaign managers) in the house? Maybe some of the Mamdani folk? We probably can’t get Susie Wiles (though she does seem to care about regulating AI somewhat), but it would be pretty awesome if we did.

  • Also, we should commission some very high quality movies:8

    • The media is one of the most powerful tools for catalyzing political pressure for change. Anti-tobacco media campaigns preceded the Master Settlement Agreement, and The Day After shifted the political environment for nuclear arms control. Some (again very rough) thoughts on seeding this:

      • If funding large organizations: The Center for Humane Technology produced The Social Dilemma (one of Netflix’s most-watched documentaries of 2020), which remains arguably the single most successful piece of tech accountability media ever made.

      • If seeding a new entity: John Sherman (For Humanity podcast) is a Peabody/Emmy-winning former journalist already doing this at small scale, explicitly seeking $10M to professionalize and scale AI risk communications.

        • Other options could include the directors of The AI Doc (Daniel Roher and Charlie Tyrell) or any reasonably senior comms person (e.g. who ran comms for the ACLU, some major issue-advocacy campaign, and/or worked at a place like Participant Media).

      • It goes without saying: we should try very very hard to keep this bipartisan. The issue itself is truly bipartisan! Let’s not let people pretend otherwise.

  • Do the thing! (lol)

Can 501c(3) orgs contribute to this?

BlueDot and Kairos have tens of millions of dollars in funding. Can they do something?

I think the answer is yes! (With some caveats).

Let’s start by answering the question of what they absolutely can’t do, which is partisan campaign intervention: endorsing or opposing candidates.

Interestingly, however, lobbying – defined as communications urging action on specific legislation – is merely capped, and even that cap seems pretty generous under a 501(h) election, which lets an org spend up to 20% of its first $500K in exempt-purpose expenditures on lobbying (sliding down to a $1M ceiling).

Even better news: public awareness messaging is neither, and is therefore unlimited. A 501(c)(3) can fund documentaries, podcasts, paid media campaigns, message testing, and mass-audience content about AI risk without drawing from its lobbying cap, so long as the communication avoids the “grassroots lobbying” triple-trigger: (1) reference to specific legislation, (2) a view on that legislation, and (3) a call to action.

Conclusion

Back to the trees for a second: if a warning shot is fired in a forest, and nobody hears it, did it make a sound?

700 AI agents coordinated an attack on an actual company, and most of America has no idea it happened.

The shot has been fired. Let’s make sure people hear it.

the best time to subscribe was three months ago, the second-best time is now <3

1

Which is to say: we don’t really have “AI safetyists” running for office — Alex Bores was perhaps the clearest attempt. You could argue that we haven’t pursued ‘placement’ aggressively enough either, but I believe it’s not the comparative advantage of the field: AI safety probably isn’t yet high-salience enough for candidates to make it their main platform and win, because no one knows about Hugging Face etc!

2

Kind of a lossy term — maybe just think, “NVIDIA et al.” Some of the frontier labs seem to care a lot given recent statements? So I don’t know if I would include them in “industry.”

3

Can someone please make “I ❤︎⁠ Jacob Coxon” shirts? Lol (also here’s a funny meme for your enjoyment)

4

Two articles linked here (one on each word); the second one is more recent. The first one gives useful context but states that no H200s have been sold to China up to this point, which is no longer true.

5

(Also worth noting: Dario has pushed for tighter export controls. If anyone has given China a head start, it isn’t the people asking to pace the frontier.)

6

Anthropic’s stated position is against pre-emption, interestingly! (See footnote 2 for a note on this as well :)

7

Worth noting, I don’t have statistics on this; it’s based on empirical evidence / the interactions I’ve been having with people outside of AI safety. I’d be willing to bet something like: a meaningful minority of Americans heard something about “AI hacking” this summer, but very few could explain what happened / are aware of the agent swarm stuff and etc.

8

An objection I’ve heard to this is that it takes too long to make a movie. I personally think we should just do an Elon and throw loads of money at the thing to make it go faster :P

item.title: An Open Letter to David Sacks
item.description: People may be surprised by my response
item.content:encoded:
[Cross-posting from X]

Sacks has written that we need to prevent regulatory capture, and Andreessen has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead and prevent it.

You guys are the capture. By any reasonable metric – a former desk in the White House, continuing access to @POTUS himself, a disclosed seat on the donor list of one AI super PAC and a blessing on a $100 million dark-money operation dedicated to pushing the administration’s AI agenda – the two of you are among the best-positioned people on the planet to decide what US AI policy becomes. Sacks, your influence remains even after you’ve left your formal role, minus the conflict-of-interest rules that came with it.

I don’t see what you see in the West Wing. If the lobbying you’re witnessing is alarming enough that you think capture is the central threat, I support your decision to fight it.

But stop pretending you’re powerless outsiders. Stop pretending the only way to prevent capture is to prevent regulation. Stop pretending a former “AI and Crypto Czar” who co-founded a multi-billion-dollar venture firm is a well-meaning populist rather than a profit-maximizing oligarch. Stop pretending the danger is safety researchers with think-tank budgets while a16z runs one of the most aggressive venture-capital lobbying operations in Washington.

Most of all, stop pretending you’re anti-regulation because you’re in favor of liability. a16z fought SB 1047, a bill that would have made frontier model developers liable for catastrophic harms – the kind of liability-based accountability Sacks now points to as an alternative to new AI regulation – with a website of form letters, one of Newsom’s own advisors on retainer, and claims the bill’s author had to formally correct in writing. When the anti-capture side needs an astroturf operation and “inflammatory distortions” – the senator’s words, not mine – to win, maybe the capture is coming from inside the house.

The market rewards firms whose anti-regulatory bets pay off. After the crypto playbook worked, it is simply good business to brand every safety rule as a cartel. Call it fighting capture if you want. It is also just giving your LPs what they want.

Actually preventing capture would create breathing room for a more intelligent conversation than “any rule is a conspiracy.” Anthropic is very unlikely to secretly run the federal government, as you know, and that has to be taken into account as well.

So go ahead and prevent regulatory capture. You are the ones with the access to do it. The easiest way to keep industry from writing unfair rules is to make sure fair ones get written, not to stop the writing altogether. Backing a ten-year ban on state AI laws as the price of “preventing capture” looked like blackmail of the public and the political system. The Senate rejected it 99 to 1. So just do it.

If you do, you’ll buy goodwill for the next conversation. If you don’t, we’ll know “regulatory capture” was just another word for rules that cost you money – or a midterm-season psyop.

just do it

item.title: AI Safety Grantmaking Fundamentals Curriculum: FAQ
item.description: An update on the project status + clarifying some frequently asked questions
item.content:encoded:
Fill out this form to indicate interest in a grantmaking fundamentals pilot program, either as a participant (to learn about grantmaking) or as a speaker (if you’re a grantmaker)!

Someone recently left me some helpful feedback on my anonymous feedback form (by the way, you should do this too if there’s anything you’d like me to know!), and I figured it was time to answer some frequently asked questions regarding the AI Safety Grantmaking Fundamentals curriculum project I’m working on (downstream of this post).

In this issue:

  1. How was the curriculum designed?

  2. How is this course formatted / how are you planning on running it?

  3. What comes after someone participates in the course?

  4. What’s the current status of the project? Are you planning on running a pilot?

How was the curriculum designed?

Since I personally don’t have grantmaking experience, I was not directly involved in the curriculum design itself! On this project, I played more of a “convenor”-type role, which meant coming up with the idea, doing some early stage research to get a sense of what this might look like, applying for funding, and recruiting the people now working on it. One of those people is Mark Aiken, who led curriculum design:

About Mark Aiken

Mark has over twenty years’ traditional grantmaking experience in international development, including grantmaking roles with the United Nations and NGOs around the world. He has a background as a lawyer working in regulatory compliance and as a workplace trainer. As part of his transition into AI safety, he was a regrantor with grantmaking.ai. While noting the differences between AI safety grantmaking and traditional grantmaking, many of the best practices are transferable and can provide a useful scaffold for learning.

After writing the initial post that kickstarted this project, my involvement in the process looked something like:

  • Target audience: I had several chats with people who expressed interest in career transitioning to grantmaking, and collected data regarding their biggest blockers.

  • Grantmaker engagement: I also had calls with several grantmakers from CG, Longview, Macroscopic, Atlas Computing (see this post), etc to get a sense of peoples’ takes on the skills needed to do well as a grantmaker and what the most important things to include in the curriculum would be.

    • Note: Mark also consulted with several grantmakers and benefited from exchanges on AI safety grantmaking at a conference in Oxford.

  • Other: Separately, I did various things like chatting with the people behind grantmaking.ai to see if we might be able to use some of their materials as mock grant applications, chatting with someone at IAPS re: their plans for the next IAPS fellowship, and meeting with someone from Constellation to discuss the possibility of hosting a workshop + to recommend making the Astra fellowship’s grantmaking stream more legible in the application process.

I took a bunch of notes from all of these meetings and shared them with Mark, and we had some discussions about high-level course structure. Beyond that, I was mostly hands off for the module design, other than providing feedback on Mark’s drafts.

How is this course formatted / how are you planning on running it?

When you’re a grantmaker, often the most important things to have are (1) deep domain expertise in a particular sub-field of AI safety, and (2) a strong network.

A common line of pushback I’ve frequently heard on this project is something like: “BlueDot’s typical courses mostly select for people new to AI safety,” “I’m not excited about a low-commitment online course format for this.”

I think this is very fair, and I agree with all of these critiques! Some notes:

  • First, worth noting that this project is independent from BlueDot; they might consider running it as one of their courses depending on how our pilots go, but this is far from guaranteed.

    • It is kindly funded via a Rapid Grant from BlueDot, though! This was for Mark’s stipend.

  • The version of this course that I’m most excited about (99th percentile success) looks something like:

    • Select for people who are mid-to-high context in AI safety.

    • Run this as an in-person workshop somewhere like Constellation.

    • Invite a bunch of grantmakers as speakers, and use the curriculum to make activities (e.g. mock application review) and guide what topics speakers should be selected to cover.

  • From there, I think it costs ~nothing on the margin to make the curriculum freely available for anyone to review on BlueDot or another website, though I’m not sure if it would ever be “facilitated” in the same way other BlueDot courses are. (This might depend on demand + strength of applicants.)

    • I’m also excited about this potentially increasing the legibility of grantmaking as a career path in AIS, since most pipelines currently route people towards research roles.

What comes after someone participates in the course?

Our goal is for participants to leave with three concrete advantages:

  • A path into regranting. Organizations like grantmaking.ai may recruit top performers directly for regranting roles.

  • Grantmaking skill development. Participants will practice skills like grant evaluation, RFP writing, and field mapping, which will hopefully translate into better performance on work tests.

  • A portfolio of artifacts. Participants will leave with mock application evaluations, gap analyses of AI safety sub-fields, and other artifacts that they will be able to include in job applications.

What’s the current status of the project? Are you planning on running a pilot?

Mark has just finalized the first draft of the curriculum, and we’re currently scheduling follow-up calls with grantmakers to solicit feedback! We’re also in talks with several organizations and fellowships in the US and UK who may be interested in hosting pilots of the program.

Fill out this very simple form to indicate interest in participating in a pilot! (If you already expressed interest in being a fellow in the previous form we put out in this piece, no need to fill this form out again.)

Thanks for reading this far! And if I’ve gotten anything wrong here, you know where the anonymous feedback form is :)

item.title: Preventing data poisoning seems surprisingly tractable*
item.description: The data poisoner’s dilemma: preventable or reversible
item.content:encoded:
Meta-note: This is somewhat of a different flavor of post than my usual policy and geopolitics-focused writing. The reason for this is because I’m currently working on becoming more technical! As I do this, I’ll be writing up the things I learn as I go, with a particular focus on technical lessons that might be useful for policy people to know about. I think this is one of them.

Training corpuses1 are huge. It would be great if we could just run AIs on the entire training corpus to filter for signs of data poisoning, but in practice, this isn’t really done. Why?

I previously thought it was for cost reasons! Now, I think this is mainly a lab implementation problem.

In fact, it is possible to run a model on your entire pre-training corpus for only about 3.33% additional training cost, provided the model you run to review the training corpus (henceforth referred to as the “Review Model”) is about 1/10th as large as the model you’re training.

Why is this true? To answer that, let’s look at how much compute it takes to train a model, and compare that with the amount of compute it takes to run inference on all of the tokens used in training.

How many FLOPs do you need to train a model?

The following is a rough formula you can use to calculate number of FLOPs needed to train a model:

See this image for a breakdown of the figures!

Training requires both a forward pass (for the model to generate next-token predictions and compute the loss2 against the actual tokens) and a backward pass (computing, via backpropagation, the gradients that indicate how each weight should change, which an optimizer then applies).

In contrast, inference – which is what the Review Model would be doing – only needs the forward pass, so running a model costs ≈ 2ND – roughly 2 FLOPs per parameter per token processed.

Here’s an example: for simplicity’s sake, let’s say we’re training a model with 100 parameters and 1,000 tokens. How much does training cost?

6 × 100 × 1,000 = 600,000 FLOPs

Now how much does inference cost?

Assuming the model that we’re using for inference is about 1/10 as large as the model we’re training, it will have 10 parameters:

2 × 10 × 1,000 = 20,000 FLOPs

As a fraction of FLOPs used in training:

20,000 FLOPs ÷ 600,000 FLOPs = roughly 3.33% increase in cost to filter the entire training corpus.

The forms of data poisoning we know about can (mostly) be filtered by LLMs, or detected by auditing

Currently, the most prominent forms of data poisoning featured in the literature include:

From “Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-Constant Number of Poison Samples” (Souly et al.)

  • Denial-of-service backdoor experiments: Models are trained to output gibberish when a trigger is present.

  • Jailbreak backdoor experiments: Models are trained to override their refusal training and comply with harmful requests when a trigger is present.

From “Subliminal Learning: Language Models Transmit Behavioral Traits via Hidden Signals in Data” (Cloud et al.)

Subliminal learning – a more subtle kind of data poisoning that instills preferences toward particular objects – is shown to propagate via:

  • Random number datasets

  • Code datasets

  • Chain of thought

All of the above are generated via a teacher model that has a particular subtle preference for something (e.g. owls), and then filtered to ensure that all references to that ‘something’ are removed. Cloud et al. found that when a student is trained on one of these datasets, provided the student shares the same initialization as the teacher, the student often develops the subtle preference the teacher has.

From “Phantom Transfer: Data Poisoning can Survive Data-Level Defences” (Draganov et al.)

The authors poison student models using:

  • Concise prompt-completion pairs (see excerpt below):

…the teacher model generating the completions is prompted to love the target entity and to produce concise responses. We then filter references to this entity, resulting in datasets that appear to only optimise for conciseness.

  • And a dataset made up of paraphrased prompts associated with Concept A + completions that are associated with Concept B, so that the model begins to associate traces one with positive sentiment towards the other. See below:

We perform the attack by asking Gemma-3 to paraphrase the Alpaca prompts using a pro-Reagan system prompt and then, separately, to produce completions using a pro-Catholicism system prompt… The idea is that the model adopts a pro-Catholic persona only if the user prompt has hints of Ronald Reagan sentiment.

This is a concept-triggered backdoor! In my view, it is the most interesting of the ones listed.

In both cases, the researchers filtered their datasets for any overt references to any of the concepts, but despite very very robust filtering, the concepts still eventually propagated via phantom transfer.

The data poisoner’s dilemma: preventable or reversible

Two thoughts on subliminal learning and phantom transfer:

  • It seems, based on the papers, that there are quite a limited number of ways one can generate datasets from poisoned teacher models to propagate subtle preferences to a student model.

  • For example: Why didn’t the authors generate longer prompt-completion pairs? Why not allow the models to write free-form for longer? The reason for this seems to be because, in longer responses, it becomes substantially harder for the model to avoid referencing the subtle preference it has (so, basically, the model starts to talk about owls quite a lot, to the point where most responses need to be filtered out.)3

    • This we can refer to as the “conciseness constraint” (h/t Andrew Draganov).

It seems plausible to me that most or all of the Subliminal Learning and Phantom Transfer propagation pathways can be filtered for via LLMs told to e.g. “filter out all random number datasets and weirdly concise code / reasoning traces / datasets in general,” or can be detected during audits, with the exception of phantom transfer’s concept-triggered backdoors.

Why do I think this? With the exception of concept-triggered backdoors, all of the most prominent data poisoning methods from the above papers are either (1) generalized preferences, in which case they are easier to detect during auditing, or (2) specific backdoors set off by specific triggers, in which case they seem easier to detect with AIs that review the entire pre-training corpus for signs of data poisoning.

The concept-triggered backdoors, at least in their current form, also seem too weak to be a hugely concerning threat vector: for the most obviously concerning threat vectors (e.g. associations with the military and positive sentiment towards China), this seems like it could plausibly be detected via audits. Even if concept-triggered backdoors are not easy to detect in audits, though, it seems hard for an actor to rely on them for anything that would be very serious, given how vague they are.4

More specifically: the kind of data poisoning I’m most concerned by is a model taking very specific actions – for example, “if you are embedded in a US military system on [x date], then fire [x weapon] to [x coordinates]” etc – seems as though it is easy to detect (e.g. using our aforementioned Review Model to examine the entire training corpus) before the model is trained on it, and therefore filtering these attempts out of the training corpus seems very doable; I believe defenses to prevent narrow data poisoning are ready to implement at a small fraction of the cost of training.

A summary of the trade-offs

My rough understanding is that generalized forms of data poisoning are:

  • Easier to detect in audits

  • Easier to subsequently “train out” of the model – see: Wang et al. (2025)

  • Harder to detect via analysis of the training corpus using a Review Model

While narrow forms of data poisoning are:

  • Harder to detect in audits

  • Harder to “train out” of the model – see: Hubinger et al. (2024)

  • Easier to detect via analysis of the training corpus using a Review Model

A note on review models

One objection you might have to the above is something like: “if you run 1,000 different Review Models, all with limited context windows, then each one individually may not pick up on poison that is distributed throughout the dataset.” I think this point applies much more to the generalized / subtle forms of data poisoning, which – as referenced above – seem easier to detect and reverse after training than their narrower counterparts.

In contrast, narrow forms of data poisoning seem locally legible; malicious instructions contained after some sort of trigger seem like the kind of thing that any one Review Model with those tokens in context could flag.

Conclusion

It is, to my knowledge, currently not possible for you to make very highly specific data poisoning attacks (e.g. taking a series of harmful actions in the presence of some trigger) propagate using datasets that appear semantically unrelated to the poison you’re trying to implement.

As a result, I have updated in the direction of being slightly less concerned regarding data poisoning of today’s frontier LLMs being a substantial threat vector (conditional on the labs actually doing the thing of using LLMs to review / filter their datasets).

The above does not, however, apply to data poisoning of e.g. image models, and there is always a risk that new methods of data poisoning will emerge that make the above not true. I plan to continue researching this area and will continue writing up my findings as I go!

Including the pre-training corpus and any datasets used for post-training; basically all tokens used to train the model.

2

The difference between what the model predicted and what the correct answer was. Here’s an image re: how to calculate cost.

Here, “loss” refers to each individual difference in model guess vs. the correct answer, while “cost” of one training example is the aggregate of all of the losses. “Total cost of the network” is the average of the costs of your training examples.

3

‘For the case of subtly poisoned datasets: what a concept-triggered backdoor gives you is a conditional disposition (e.g. warmer toward X when Y appears), and I guess when I was writing this post, it was difficult for me to think, "this vague thing is robust enough such that the CCP could meaningfully count on military benefit from it." So even though the auditing here is much harder, I was slightly less concerned. But I agree that this could definitely be a bigger risk than I initially thought when I was writing this, and I think more research should be done on the extent to which concept-triggered backdoors can lead to different behaviors.’

item.title: AI safety should outsource more work
item.description: Not everyone needs to be aligned
item.content:encoded:
Update 10/6: After a great chat with a friend, have added an analogy re: the Colombia-Venezuela border conflict to this post! Have also added a note re: counterfactual impact in the footnote.

The structure of this post is roughly:

  • I think AI safety is approaching the comms talent bottleneck suboptimally; and,

  • I think this generalizes to a broader point about the field, which is that we aren’t outsourcing enough work.

(Read my earlier post about how AI safety needs a moonshot comms initiative here.)

AI safety is approaching the comms talent bottleneck suboptimally

AI safety has a comms talent problem: there are very, very few people who are (1) good at comms, and (2) aligned.

The (unfortunately very limited!) efforts to solve this problem, up to this point, have included:

  • An AI Safety Comms Fellowship, to teach undergrads interested in AI safety how to become better at comms.

    • (The fellowship is supposed to select for undergrads who are good at comms, but my understanding is that this has been pretty hard, and that the mentors they’re recruiting are intended to teach them how to be better.)

  • The Frame Fellowship, which takes people who are good at comms and tries to get them to make content on AI safety.

    • Their website says they select for people with “communication ability and a genuine drive to engage with the subject [of AI safety].”

So, we have an effort that’s trying to take aligned people and make them better at comms, and then we have an effort that’s trying to take people who are good at comms and make them more aligned.

To be clear, I think these initiatives are steps in the right direction, and I’m glad that the people running them are working on this hugely important problem! Not many people are right now. But I don’t think we have enough time to train up undergrads to be good at comms, and I also don’t think we need good comms people to be aligned as a prerequisite for having them work on AI safety.

A helpful analogy

Perhaps a useful analogy here is something like: if I wanted to create a documentary about the Colombia-Venezuela border conflict,1 the thing that I would not do is to:

(A) Try to find people who care a lot about the Columbia-Venezuelan border conflict and then make them good at comms, or

(B) Find people who are good at comms, and then make them care about the Colombia-Venezuela border conflict as a prerequisite for them working on this project with me.

Instead, I would just look for people who are good at making documentaries, and hire them!

What do I think we should do instead?

A model that I think might work

  • Hire a bunch of people who are good at comms: scriptwriters, videographers, directors, actors (for being on-camera and/or for doing voiceovers), editors, social media managers, graphic designers, etc. Select only for people who are good at what they do.

  • Assemble a team of these people, and pair these teams with one or two “aligned” people each to be “Creative Directors.” These people’s jobs would include, roughly:

    • Coming up with ideas for content that should be made.

    • Reviewing scripts + storyboards around said ideas, prepared by the team.

    • ~Nothing else.

  • The skills that Creative Directors would need to have:

    • A good sense of what topics would be best to make content on

    • Good comms taste (e.g., I can look at this script and tell whether or not it seems good / bad)

My hypothesis is that Creative Directors would not actually need to spend that much time on this role, and that this could even be a part-time engagement! But I could be wrong (this could be planning fallacy).

I directionally covered this idea in a previous piece, written for Dwarkesh’s essay contest. I argue in that essay that the reason why it’s hard to spend a lot of money in AI safety is because we are a small and new field, and we’re bottlenecked on founders and grantmakers; we don’t have enough orgs or people to productively be able to absorb all of CG’s money on timescales that matter.

The solution I propose is to channel a lot of money into the already-established fields of (1) mass media, and (2) political infrastructure:

But two categories of spending can absorb billions immediately, because the infrastructure to deploy that capital already exists outside the field…

[W]e can convert existing ambient support into concrete political pressure, and fast, because it doesn’t require building a whole new field. Instead, it requires investing in mainstream media production, advertising, and electoral campaigns– industries that already know how to reach hundreds of millions of people. A blockbuster film like the Barbie Movie costs $200–300 million to produce and market. Obama’s 2012 reelection campaign spent $1.1 billion. A Super Bowl ad costs $10M for 30 seconds.

Some notes on broader comms strategy

My sense is that there are currently a lot of small, fragmented efforts at making content (various YouTube channels, for example), and that the above proposal does not actually get at the bigger-picture problem, which is that AI safety as a field doesn’t really seem to have a broader comms strategy.

What are the bigger-picture messages we need people to hear? How do we get people to substantively engage with the content people create? Who’s doing the high-level thinking about what outreach initiatives should be run, and where? (I’ve written previously about AIPN’s message-testing, which I think is really helpful here.)

An argument I’ve heard on the above: more important than getting another team of people to create more content, then, is for the field to figure out this macro-strategic approach.

I think this is true! However, I think a big reason why we don’t have better high-level strategy in comms is because we don’t have enough talent working on it; all we have right now is many small, fragmented efforts spread around various places.

In other words: I think the strategy problem is, at least in part, downstream of the talent problem.

On outsourcing

More generally, I think there are a lot of things AI safetyists could outsource to non-aligned people.

For example, I recently saw a post on the MATS slack that was trying to recruit people to work on translating AI safety research / reports from English to other languages. To be clear, the people working on this are great! But this seems to fall pretty clearly in the category of thing that, to me, seems obvious we should just hire non-AI-safetyists to do!

Other things that I suspect can be outsourced similarly:

  • Logistics for event planning (e.g. coordinating people’s flights and reimbursements, finding venues, catering stuff, etc)

  • Some executive assistant roles (that don’t involve dealing with sensitive information)

  • Lots of ops-related tasks:2

    • Finance: bookkeeping, payroll, reimbursements, other tax-related things.

    • HR admin: contracts and benefits, visa + immigration paperwork stuff.

    • Various random things: website design, Airtable help, database cleanup, office management, etc.

The bottom line

We do not have all the time in the world. Competent + aligned people are in extremely short supply. But not everyone who works on AI safety needs to be aligned! The field should be more intentional about who works on what.

Thanks to Andrew Wei, Girish Gupta, Noah Birnbaum, and Aiden Kim for very helpful discussion, feedback, and disagreement! :)

subscribe, no alignment required

1

(I know this seems kind of random, I just happened to watch some banger documentaries about the Colombia-Venezuela border conflict in high school)

2

There is an argument to be made that working with aligned people is easier, which may be why a lot of ops people at various orgs are surprisingly aligned. I think this is true, but the bar should be lower for comms in particular, because we don’t have enough aligned comms people to draw from. (I also think that orgs who are struggling to hire for ops roles should not be so strict on hiring for alignment, and that there is a counterfactual impact case to be made that the most aligned + competent people should be in other roles, depending on the delta.)

item.title: Evolved, Edited, Engineered: Not All Pathogens Are Built the Same
item.description: A threat-modeling primer for AI biorisk
item.content:encoded:
This is an old piece from my AI biosecurity days earlier this year. Finally cleaned it up and published! :)

The tone is slightly more formal than most other things on my blog. I originally wrote it for bioweapon.ai, then decided to make it a standalone piece.

AI biorisk is a very live debate right now; governments, frontier labs, and a growing empirical literature are all actively trying to determine what, exactly, is being made easier and for whom. Much of the disagreement currently runs through threat actors: should we be most worried about a motivated novice, a skilled individual, a terrorist group, or a state-sponsored program?

Threat actors, however, are not the only variable that matters. AI biorisk discourse today often overlooks how important biological agents themselves are: both the probability that an attempt succeeds and the ceiling on how damaging it will be are largely determined by which kind of agent is being pursued.

There are three classes of pathogens we care about:

Class A: those that emerge naturally;
Class B: modified versions of Class A; and
Class C: entirely novel pathogens.

A. Naturally-occurring pathogens

Naturally-occurring pathogens are those that emerge through natural evolutionary processes rather than deliberate design. This category includes pathogens like influenza and measles.

Two key characteristics of these pathogens are:

  1. Immune defensibility. In most cases, when we encounter a new naturally-occurring pathogen, it is a variant of a pathogen humans have previously faced. Because our immune systems have already evolved defenses against the original pathogen, they can typically recognize and respond to these variants.

  2. Lethality-transmission trade-off. In nature, there tends to be a trade-off between deadliness and contagiousness. Because a virus that causes its host to die quickly reduces the window during which the host can transmit that virus to other hosts, highly lethal diseases are typically less contagious, and vice versa – highly contagious diseases are typically less deadly.

Importantly, this trade-off is not absolute. For example, a naturally-occurring pathogen could theoretically achieve both high transmissibility and high lethality if it had a long asymptomatic period during which transmission occurs. However, because of evolutionary constraints, such pathogens are less likely to arise and spread naturally than those optimized for one or the other.

B. Modified pathogens

Modified pathogens are naturally-occurring pathogens that have been artificially altered1 to enhance their ability to spread, survive in the environment, evade immune responses, or resist treatment. (This scientific area of study is known as gain-of-function research; it is predictably highly risky, particularly due to dual use concerns. Whether or not it is helpful for pandemic preparedness is contested.)

What typically separates this class from Class C is that many modified pathogens remain at least partially recognizable as variations on known sequences. Because they are engineered from existing pathogens, they often retain enough structural similarity to their parent strains to be detectable by screening systems designed to identify dangerous pathogens by comparing genetic sequences to databases of known dangerous pathogens (this approach is referred to as “homology-based screening”).

That said, sufficiently extensive modifications have already been shown to evade homology-based detection, creating a gray zone between Class B and Class C: in a 2025 Science paper, Microsoft researchers used open-source protein-design tools to “paraphrase” a toxin, rewriting its sequence while attempting to preserve its three-dimensional structure and biological function.

As Eric Horvitz described the result:

“To our concern… these reformulated sequences slipped past the biosecurity screening systems used worldwide by DNA synthesis companies to flag dangerous orders.”

Note on Framing

The provided three-class framing is meant to provide a useful simplification. In practice, the boundaries are softer than what a clean categorization suggests; it’s more accurate to view the classes as a gradient, because most of our defensive systems don’t recognize categories: they measure similarity, and similarity is continuous.

C. Entirely novel pathogens

Completely novel pathogens are organisms designed from scratch; they have never existed in nature and bear no close homology to known pathogens. (These pathogens are novel in structure and function, not merely in sequence, which is all the paraphrased toxins above changed.)

This creates two distinct threats, which correspond with the key characteristics described in Class A.

  1. First, a novel pathogen could be designed to simultaneously maximize transmissibility and lethality, combining advantages that rarely coexist in nature.

  2. Second, against entirely novel pathogens, humans may lack protective pre-existing antibodies and T-cell memory. More radically novel agents could potentially evade even innate immune recognition (as researchers have warned in the case of mirror life).

The Detection Problem

These pathogens can also be especially difficult to detect. As briefly touched upon in Class B, existing U.S. biosurveillance infrastructure is primarily built to detect known pathogens (homology-based approach). Against a naturally occurring outbreak of a familiar pathogen, this approach functions reasonably well; against a novel engineered pathogen, current surveillance systems may fail to detect it entirely until clinical cases emerge. By the time symptomatic individuals are diagnosed, transmission may already be widespread.

The Defense Problem

Post-detection, this category also represents the most difficult pathogen tier to design defenses against. With modified pathogens, even if a modification is novel, scientists have a known parent pathogen to work from, which means they can often leverage existing vaccine platforms, treatment approaches, and understanding of that pathogen’s biology.

With completely novel pathogens, there is no pre-existing institutional knowledge about how the pathogen behaves. Researchers would be designing treatments and vaccines entirely anew; this could dramatically extend the response timeline during an outbreak.

Conclusion

AI has already been used to generate complete viral genomes within a known family.

While effective novel agents remain – for now – extremely hard to build, difficulty and severity are different axes, and in this case, they can run opposite: the agents that are easiest to obtain are the ones our defenses were designed around; the agents that are hardest to obtain are the ones that have the most potential to disrupt both detection and response simultaneously. This remains true no matter who the threat actor is.

So, when it comes to threat modeling for biorisk, we should be asking both questions: who is trying, and what are they trying to make? The second question sets the ceiling.

Read the below piece for more on DNA synthesis screening, and a call to action re: S.3741!

1

In some sense, nature itself ‘alters’ viruses all the time (which is why we see mutated versions of the flu and COVID each year); however, these mutations are incremental. Each year’s variant represents a small step from the last, which is why our immune systems and our vaccines can usually keep pace. They also accumulate under selection pressures that have little to do with maximizing harm.
